speechtext: Mr. Speaker, some time ago a question was asked in this house with regard to the proceedings taken by the government of the United States to extradite Frank Grigware, otherwise known as Frank Lawrence Fahey, who was residing in Jasper, Alberta. The community in which he lived, the board of trade and many private individuals made representations to the government as to his excellent citizenship and the long time that he had lived in .that locality with credit and distinction to himself and to the community. These representations were conveyed to the offices of the Prime Minister and forwarded to the minister at Washington, who in turn transmitted them to the Secretary of State of the United States. I am just advised by the legation at Washington that the attorney general of the United States has discontinued extradition proceedings against Grigware. subtopic: SUGAR TAX

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SUGAR TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), who is the acting Minister of Finance, to an article which appeared in this morning's Montreal Gazette concerning the sugar tax. It reads as follows:
Information reaching the Montreal board of trade yesterday from sources closely linked' to the wholesale grocery trade was to the effect that in the coming fall the excise tax on sugar will be cut altogether by the federal government.
May I ask the Prime Minister if there is anything behind that statement?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SUGAR TAX
speechtext:
The article to which the hon.
member has referred affords me an opportunity to make some observations which I think every hon. member will agree should be made. The press of the country carries on an agitation based upon some suggestion made by someone interested in a given course of events. The result is that petitions are circulated, in many instances, which are signed and presented to governments, and then it is said that something is to be done at a given time-that the excise tax on cigarettes is to be removed, that the sugar tax is to be lessened. All this is circulated throughout the country to the detriment of the government of the country and to the administration not of this government but the administration of the affairs and business of the country.
I can only say that that story is as devoid of any foundation in fact as any story I know of could be. Yet the effect of it will be that the next thing we will hear will be that "As the tax is to come back on a given day we trust you will make provision for those who have stores on hand;" and it will continue to go on in that way for weeks. In some countries this practice has become so intolerable that they have passed legislation making it an offence to circulate false news of that kind, for reasons which I think commend themselves to every hon. member in this house. The result has been that there has been a curtailment of the circulation of this type of news. It is not news; it is rumour. And it makes no difference how many times you contradict it, you can never overtake it. There will be people in remote parts of the country who will hear about or read these articles, and they will believe that something is contemplated. Then, if some
Coal Investigation

action is taken in six months or, say, next year in the budget, it will be alleged that someone had advance information in respect to it.
I can only protest, not in the name of a government, or this government, but in the name of all governments in Canada, whose task is always great, against the circulation of rumours in the public press-and especially in view of the fact that the carriage of papers through the mails of this country represents a loss to the taxpayers of Canada of, it is estimated, not less than $6,000,000 per year.
Under the circumstances I think I am not going too far when I suggest that at least those who administer the affairs of the country, whether they be a Liberal government, a Conservative government, or any other form of government, are entitled to that consideration from the public press with respect to the conduct of public business which will not allow rumours, such as that to which the hon. member has just referred, to be circulated throughout the country in reputable journals, and believed to be true.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to
comment-I was going to say on one of the proposed amendments, but it is rather an omitted amendment, if I might call it that. I congratulate the minister upon having had the amendments printed. I am sure that it will facilitate the passage of the bill. I assume, however, that the amendments printed are all that he proposes to introduce, and that no others will be permitted or encouraged.
I venture to point out one feature which I do not think has been touched on at all in this house up to date, and in which this bill is wholly lacking as compared with the British act, and that is in a provision as regards contracts. The minister is well aware that in big business arrangements we do not do business like selling peanuts over the counter. Arrangements have to be made months, and sometimes years, ahead. Contracts have to be entered into. It is quite a common thing especially in seasonal industries for the whole output to be contracted for before the season begins. In some cases the banks hesitate to finance the industry unless that arrangement is made. I would like to ask what effect the minister thinks this bill will have on industry as a whole if it is found that under it, it is almost impossible to contract ahead.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) a day or two ago instanced the case of a business man doing business in Brazil and wanting to make a contract. There are other cases of the same kind. For instance, a man comes along and wants to buy the whole output of a pilchard plant on the west coast of Vancouver island. Is that producer to say to his prospective customer, " I am very sorry. I would like to sell, but I cannot do it. I can tell you next October whether I shall be allowed to do so or not." The minister may have some answer to that, and I shall be glad to hear it when he speaks
I want to give an illustration of what the British government thought essential to take care of such conditions. I refer hon. gentlemen to page 262 of the Agricultural
Marketing Act-Mr. Neill

Marketing Act of 1931, section 8, which covers two pages and a little more, and contains provisions to take care of conditions of that kind. I need not read it all. Suffice it to say that any contract entered into before the going into force of that act, or any contract entered into afterwards, provided it was not done with the deliberate intention of evading the act, is entirely taken care of. I refer the minister to the section I have quoted. In one instance it says that no person shall be liable to any penalty for contravention of any scheme in force under the act if he proves that the contravention was necessary for the performance of a contract and providing it was not done in evasion of the act. I do think that there should be some provision, and a very definite provision for that situation here because, I repeat, you cannot do business from hand to mouth. You must look ahead. Take the case of a contract for flour for shipment to the orient. Has the shipper to be put in the position where he can only say, "I do not know. I would like to do it but I have to get the consent of the board"-not of an unknown board, but of a board that we do not know the composition of, or how it will be composed, or its numbers, and we know very little about its ideas. Perhaps that vagueness is necessary on account of the dual jurisdiction, but nevertheless it makes it all the more necessary that some provision of the kind I suggest should be provided.
While I am on my feet I would like to allude to the remarks which the minister made yesterday with regard to the protection of the consumer. He said that there were three safeguards, first, that the scheme had to be approved by the minister and by the governor in council; but the minister and the governor in council are practically the same because what the minister recommends to his colleagues more or less automatically goes through except in very exceptional circumstances. So that brings it down-I do not wish to be unfair and say to the whim or caprice of the minister, but to the determination of a single minister, and that is not a sufficient safeguard to the consumer. It is not sufficient to have it left to one man whose judgment perhaps is based on insufficient information as to what is necessary to protect the consumer in that particular industry, or phase of industry, of which the minister may have absolutely no personal knowledge. If the minister has beliefs and opinions on that matter, why not put some provision in the bill for the protection of the consumer?

The second safeguard which the minister claimed existed was that there was no pricefixing but a regulating of the rate at which the stuff goes on to the market. I think the two are synonymous. If not, what is the purpose of the bill? Is not the bill to help the producers get a better price? I think the hon. member for Ontario yesterday exploded that theory by showing that, if you do such and so, the price will regulate itself. If people are prevented from selling, the result must be to stimulate the price directly or indirectly.
The third safeguard to which the minister alluded was that there was part 2 of the bill which gives power to control undue charges. Well, I do not think that is a logical argument at all. That refers to spreads, not original prices. The minister no doubt was alluding to sections 18, 19, 20 and 21, which give power to investigate spreads between producer and consumer. By the way, the minister is taking the teeth out of that by his amendment when he is limiting the committee simply to giving a report of what is in their opinion an unjust spread. The committee has not now the power to determine that the spread is unjust. It is not even a definite report. It gives only their opinions. Therefore, I suppose it follows that the provisions of section 21, the penalty section, will not apply as that section derives its authority from sections 19 and 20. Although there may be some outlet by way of the Combines Investigation Act, so far as this bill is concerned its teeth have been largely drawn. The committee is to investigate what spread is detrimental to or against the interests of the public in that it is excessive or results in undue enhancement of prices. This part of the bill only refers to spreads made by the middleman, to which reference has been made. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) has said that there was no protection given to the consumer. The prices given to the producer may be unduly high but the minister's argument is that action can be taken apparently under the Combines Investigation Act. The powers in this bill are to some degree wholly divergent from and contradictory to, the restrictions imposed by the Combines Investigation Act.
What does Great Britain do about it? There they have a consumers' committee, and this is not a committee existing only in the mind of the minister. The British act reads;
A consumers' committee shall consist of a chairman and of not less than six other members, who shall be such persons as appear to the minister, after consultation with the board

Marketing Act-Mr. Neill
of trade and, as to one member, with the Cooperative Union, to represent the interests of the consumers of all the products the marketing of which is for the time being regulated by schemes approved by the minister.
It is a well known fact that the board of trade in England functions in a manner entirely different from our local boards of trade. The board of trade there alluded to is practically a department of government. This committee is charged with the duty of considering and reporting to the minister on the effect of any scheme approved by the minister, which is for the time being in force, on consumers of the regulated product. If necessary, another committee can be set up under the British act. This is a committee of investigation and shall consist of a chairman and four other members. That committee is charged with the duty of going into the statements made by the original committee. That committee has full power to go to any of these boards and examine their books, and so on. A report is then made to the minister. If the committee of investigation reports to the minister that any provision of a scheme is contrary to the interests of consumers or the interests of any persons affected by the scheme and is not in the public interest, the minister, after consulting with the board of trade, may by order make such amendments as are thought necessary or revoke the scheme. Those are pretty drastic powers to be carried out on the recommendation of the first committee as endorsed by the second investigating committee. The minister may then revoke the whole scheme if he thinks a consumer is getting what we call a raw deal.
If amendments such as these were introduced into this bill we would be given more encouragement to vote in its favour, but when we see the wide divergence between this bill and the protections given under the British act, it makes us wonder whether the whole thing is not just a piece of window dressing to look at, to admire and to point to rather than something that is to be carried out. I hope I am not doing the minister and the government an injustice in saying that. Why not make the thing workable and practicable? Does not the minister think that there should be some protection for existing contracts, those made either immediately before or immediately after the passing of this bill, in order to maintain the ordinary channels of trade?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I shall deal with the hon. member's questions as nearly in order as I can. First, the amendments to this bill are not a closed book, as he suggests.
Secondly, I feel that all local boards will be anxious to facilitate all contracts rather than to break them. As far as protection to the consumer is concerned, what protection has he at the present time which he would not have after this bill is passed? The hon. member has suggested that the chief purpose of the bill is to raise prices, but I have always maintained that the chief purpose is to stabilize prices.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: The same thing.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Very different. For example, under present conditions it is quite possible-I believe hon. members will agree with me when I say that it has been done- that forces outside the control of the producer and outside the welfare of the consumer may	bring	prices	down to an	abnormally low level. Stocks may be accumulated in the hands of a few, and prices raised higher than	would	have	been possible	hadthe flow of	goods	been	regulated and	theconsumer forced to pay more than he otherwise would have to pay. Under this bill all products	will go forward according to
grade and in a more regular manner and prices and markets will be stabilized.
With reference to the protection given in Great Britain to the consumers: Consumers' committees are set up; they report their objections to the minister, who takes them before the governor in council, after consulting with the board of trade. Under this bill we have the power to revoke schemes and withdraw authority from the local board. We have just as much power over our local board as is given under the British marketing act. We have the power to regulate the spread between what the producer gets and what the consumer pays. At the present time there are very few ways of controlling that.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
It comes back to the fact that the minister has sole control; he can kill or he can keep alive. He may be satisfied to assume that power, but I would not care to be in his position. It is true that the bill says he can revoke, but there is no machinery provided whereby the consumer can be vocal in expressing his wrongs. Such machinery is provided for in the British act, under which there is the consumers' committee and the additional investigating committee. Where is the machinery in this bill? I may approach the minister and say that such a thing is wrong and he may or may not take action-. He has no facilities for doing so. This bill is not at all compatible with the British bill, but if that is his determination-

Marketing Act-Mr. Woodsworth

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: The hon. member states that there are no facilities for taking action. What more facility is necessary than the power to withdraw, if necessary, all authority from the local board?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I believe that is expressed in section 5, but it is expressed in a very general way. I think any minister would hesitate to destroy completely the work of a board simply on the say-so of Tom Jones. Tom Jones' complaint is not given any authority or power. He may apply to the minister and the minister's deputy may decide that there is nothing in the complaint. There is no real machinery provided whereby the consumer can express his wrongs. The only way he can speak is by personal letter to the minister.
The minister said that any local board would be glad to facilitate contracts, but I do not know why they should be. We do not know what these boards may be like. They may be flushed with their authority. They are put in power and the: first thing they will want to do is to control things as much as possible. It would be a deterrent rather than a help to their operations to have existing contracts. They certainly will not be friendly and sympathetic to people who have made prior contracts. But at any rate their powers begin when the board is approved by the minister, and there will be existing contracts then. There will be no provision however to take care of them. We cannot be very far wrong if we follow the British act, not in its letter and entirety, for their conditions are different, but in its general spirit. They have a very fine sense of making laws that are workable, laws that fit in with the general temper of the people, and it is because laws meet with the approval of the vast mass of the people that they are so well observed in Britain. It is because the laws are so constructed as to afford every facility to anyone to get redress for any grievance which he may feel. I think there should be provision in this act to take care of existing contracts, before the bill goes into effect.

Coming from western Canada, I am interested in this bill particularly in so far as it applies to the marketing of wheat. Wheat forms probably ninety per cent of the products of the western farmer. Will the minister tell us how, under present conditions, this act when applied to wheat will help the farmer to get any more for his product? If it is going to help the farmer to get a fraction of a cent more for his wheat, then I am prepared to support it in every way.
We all know the conditions which the farmers in the west are faced with to-day. True, the farmer in the west is a little better off than he was last year. Last year when he produced a dollar's worth of commodities he lost 50 cents; to-day he does not lose quite so much, only about 25 cents. In other words, last year it cost him $1 to produce 50 cents worth of his commodities and today it costs him $1 to produce 75 cents worth. He is therefore just a little bit better off, but it will take a long time before he is on his feet again, and if this bill will help to put him on his feet once more I am ready to support it in every way.
Some people say that the great carryover of wheat has been all due to the Liberal policies that were in force from 1921 to 1929. They say that we lost our market under Liberal rule, that all restrictions placed against our wheat were put into effect while the Liberals were in power, and that no restrictions have been imposed since. Well, let us look at the facts. I will deal with wheat, taking a few countries, the major importing countries. What do we find in France? On July 1, 1930, when the Liberal government
went out of power, the duty against our wheat going into France was 85 cents a bushel; on the 1st of May, 1934 there was a duty of $1.44 per bushel in force against us. That increase has come about under the Conservative government. For the last four or five years we have not had a crop of wheat and yet our carryovers have been piling up year after year. In Germany, on July 1, 1930 there was a duty of 97i cents per bushel against our wheat; on the 1st of May, 1934 the German duty was $2.69-an increase piled up since this government came into power. Take Italy, which is another great importer. On July 1, 1930, the Italian duty against our wheat was 87 cents per bushel, and to-day that duty has been increased to $1.74 per bushel. Yet they tell us that no increase has been made in the duties against Canadian wheat going to other countries.
What about Belgium? On July 1, 1930, Belgium had a duty of one per cent ad valorem; to-day they have a duty of thirteen cents a bushel plus two and a half per cent ad valorem. What about Spain? On July 1, 1930, Spain had a duty of $1.10 a bushel; to-day they have a duty so fixed that the price of wheat in Spain shall always be at least $1.98 per bushel. What about China? On July 1, 1930, China had no duty on wheat; it was free. To-day the duty is ten cents a bushel including the surtax.
But that is not all. These importing countries have placed other restrictions, milling restrictions and quotas against our wheat. What do we find with regard to France? On July 1, 1930, three per cent of foreign wheat was allowed in all milling flour for domestic use; to-day no foreign wheat is allowed in domestic flour. On July 1, 1930, Germany allowed 70 per cent of foreign wheat in her flour; to-day only three per cent of foreign wheat is allowed in her domestic flour. On July 1, 1930, Italy had no restrictions; to-day they allow only one per cent of foreign wheat to be used in domestic flour.
The whole answer is that the duties and the restrictions which this government has piled up against the products of other nations have made us lose many of our markets. Let us look at what the Commercial Intelligence Journal of May 5, 1934, has to say in regard to Canadian wheat imported into Switzerland:
Since the war Switzerland's annual imports of Canadian wheat have been close to 10,000,000 bushels. Taking into consideration its population of approximately 4,000.000, it has thus been one of the best per capita markets in the
Marketing Act-Mr. Donnelly

world. Under normal economic conditions this trade would continue. Switzerland has, however, found it necessary to restrict imports from countries such as Canada and the United States with which there is a heavy unfavourable trade balance, and to divert it to other cereal-producing states with whom compensation agreements can be made.
Then they give a list of Switzerland's wheat imports, which shows that during the months of January, February and March, 1933, she imported from Canada 83,015 metric tons and for the months of January, February and March, 1934, only 24,886 metric tons. The article continues:
During the first quarter of 1933 Canada supplied 67-5 per cent of Switzerland's total wheat imports. For the same period of 1934 the figure had shrunk to roughly 28 per cent, a loss of 58,129 metric tons. For the second quarter of 1934 it is reported that quota allotments will allow Swiss millers to use only ten per cent of Canadian wheat, . . .
Assuming this to be the case, only about fifteen per cent of Switzerland's total imports for 1934 will come from Canada in comparison with 47-13 per cent in 1933 and fifty-two per cent in 1932. It is not improbable therefore that Canadian grain exporters will have to face the possibility of losing a market for as much as 175,000 metric tons or 6,431,250 bushels of wheat
That is lost in Switzerland alone. That is what has caused our markets throughout the world to be lost. The other day France gave us the answer. I wish to call the minister's attention to a statement made by an eminent authority with regard to interference with freedom of the business of a country. I refer him to a book entitled The English Constitution -written by Walter Bagehot. He speaks first about bureaucracy,-and if ever a bill was intended or calculated in the final result to build up a bureaucracy, I say it is this one. If the committee will permit I shall read what the author has to say in this regard:
Not only does a bureaucracy thus tend to under-government, in point of quality; it tends to over-government, in point of quantity. The trained official hates the rude, untrained public. He thinks that they are stupid, ignorant, reckless-that they cannot tell their own interest-that they should have the leave of the office before they do anything. Protection is the natural inborn creed of every official body, free trade is an extrinsic idea, alien to its notions, and hardly to be assimilated with life; and it is easy to see how an accomplished critic, used to a free and active life, could thus describe the official.
And this is the description.
"Every imaginable and real social interest" says Mr. Laing, "religion, education, law, police, every branch of public or private business, personal liberty to move from place to place, even from parish to parish within the same jurisdiction; liberty to engage in any branch of trade or industry, on a small or large scale, all the objects, in short, in which body, mind, and capital can be employed' in civilized society, were gradually laid hold of for the employment and support of functionaries, were centralized in bureaux, were superintended, licensed, inspected, reported upon, and interfered with by a host of officials scattered over the land, and maintained at the public expense, yet with no conceivable utility in their duties. They are not, however, gentlemen at large, enjoying salary without service. They are under a semi-military discipline. In
Bavaria, for instance, the superior civil functionary can place his inferior functionary under house-arrest, for neglect of duty, or other offence against civil functionary discipline. In Wurtemberg, the functionary cannot marry without leave from his superior. Voltaire says, somewhere, that, 'the art of government is to make two-thirds of a nation pay all it possibly can pay for the benefit of the other third.' This is realized in Germany by the functionary system."
I shall not read it at length, but it goes on to say:
The functionaries are not there for the benefit of the people, but the people for the benefit of the functionaries. All this machinery of funetionarism, with its numerous ranks and gradations in every district, filled with a staff of clerks and expectants in every department looking for employment, appointments, or promotions, was intended to be a new support of the throne in the new social state of the continent; a third class, in connection with the people by their various official duties of interference in all public or private affairs, yet attached by their interests to the kingly power.
And this is the last reference I intend to make.
The Beamptenstand, or functionary class,, was to be equivalent to the class of nobility, gentry, capitalists, and men of larger landed property than the peasant-proprietors, and was to make up in numbers for the want of individual weight and influence. In France, at the expulsion of Louis Philippe, the civil functionaries were stated to amount to 807.030 individuals. This civil army was more than double of the military. In Germany, this class is necessarily more numerous in proportion to the population, the landwehr system imposing many more restrictions than the conscription on the free action of the people, and requiring more officials to manage it, and the semi-feudal jurisdictions and forms of law requiring much more writing and intricate forms of procedure before the courts than the Code Napoleon.

May I say to him that I think it is a diametrically opposite principle. The principle of local option is that everyone in a community determines whether or not there is to be local option. Under this measure, only an interested occupational group determines what regulations shall apply. The correct parallel would be if local option in a given community were decided by, say, only those who were intemperate or wished to drink as they please. If only that class of people were to be given the right to decide whether or not everyone was to have the right to drink as he pleased, you would have an exact parallel. Take it the other way. The producers of these byproducts are not always the original producers. For instance, the original producer or fisherman does not produce cod liver oil. The lobster packer produces tamale but the original fisherman does not. I shall not refer to the seal fishing on the Pacific coast or at other places, but considerable is done in the maritime provinces. The man who hunts the seals does not extract the oil. In the case of fishcake, the man who does the fishing sells the product to the consumer but the sardine packing industry also manufactures fishcake from the products of the fisherman. In the case of fertilizer, there is natural fertilizer and manufactured fertilizer. Herring fry are found along the Atlantic coast. If the wind is favourable these are found in windrows three or four feet high by two to three feet wide running for miles along the shore. That product is saved and used as fertilizer but is not put through any process of manufacture. Now what group will handle that? Will it be the farmer, the primary producer from the soil, or will it be those engaged in the fishing industry? With all due respect to the minister and his attempt to do what he thinks is right, I confess that I am scared that

Marketing Act-Mr. Veniot
so far as the fishing industry is concerned he does not know where he is drifting; if he did he would not allow the fishing industry to go into this bill. The bill is inoperative, and before he undertakes to bring the fishing industry within its provisions I would strongly advise him to consult the Department of Fisheries. In that department there are men of vast experience, experts who have studied the industry in all its details, who know the history of fishing, who have followed up the fish from the time the fry is sent out until it is ready for the market. In the maritimes there are associations that have made a special study of the fishing industry under the direction of the Department of Fisheries in Ottawa. And let me say this for the department. Prior to my time at Ottawa, and since, I have had wide experience with the officials of that department and I can say that there are no officials in any department of the government that pay more attention and give better service to an industry than do the officials of the Department of Fisheries to the Canadian fishing industry. We have a biological institution that studies very carefully the history of the fish and reports if not weekly at any rate monthly to the department the requirements of the fishermen, suggesting to the department what should be done to encourage these men to improve their conditions, and to find markets for their product. In the department here there is an organization that indicates to the fishermen the time when the fish will school, as we say in the industry: in what sections of the country and at what dates and tides it pays the fishermen to go into deep waters to catch mackerel; and so on. From the biological office there is given to the department information which indicates the best localities for codfish, and information as to conditions on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland is also available. In the department there is an organization that stimulates the fishermen to greater efforts than they have made in the past.
Under the last government the department organized a circle of fishermen's associations, not only to study the marketing business and the curing of fish, but to instruct fishermen in better methods of attaining their ends; and all this information is in the Fisheries department. All the necessary organization exists in that department. Why then impose upon the fishermen this law that places upon them, restrictions which they cannot carry out?
I am not speaking in any political sense this afternoon. If I had politics in view I would say, "Put the bill through as it is," because it would mean my election by acclamation in

The interpretation distinctly declares that "board" means the federal board, and it also states that local board shall mean so and so. 14. Not satisfied with having broken the promises made to the farmers in 1930, to-day, by bill No. 51, as sections 14 and 21 testify, the government threatens the farmers with a fine or imprisonment if they do not comply with its marketing act; it is an insult to the farming class.
In 1932, sir, previous to the Imperial Economic Conference, held in Ottawa, the farmers, seeing that their distress had increased during the two years that this administration had been in office, considered it proper to suggest to the government what they themselves thought would remedy their situation, so that it might be discussed at the conference. Almost 2,000 delegates representing the farming class of all parts of Canada

An act to improve the methods and practices involved in the marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provision in connection therewith.

up by full parliamentary responsibility. I am for a marketing bill which will rest on the freedom of thought and action of the producers concerned, which will be built from the foundation up and not from the top down, which will be democratic and not bureaucratic. I am more than pleased to witness the somewhat changed attitude of some hon members sitting to my right. It seems that now there is not very much difference between the contending factions in the committee. In fact, we have almost reached a stage of unanimity, and possibly with one or two further slight amendments the bill might go from the committee and, after third reading, be adopted as the unanimous legislation of the House of Commons. I am only too pleased to observe that I should be happy to do anything within my power to bring about unanimity. However, I have no desire in view of the statements that were made here last night and this afternoon to get into any controversy over the different aspects of this bill because it appears that controversy is almost a thing of the past so far as many phases of this bill are concerned. We are all agreed that in a measure of this kind there has to be a certain amount of compulsion or coercion, and the idea of a particular group voting for a new kind of economic council being formed is one I think that is accepted generally. Some are fearful because it will be occupational groups who will vote for a scheme under this bill, instead of the community as a whole. We are living in an age where because of economic

conditions we are compelled to experiment along different lines perhaps than have been followed in the past.
I rose to point out that there have been a number of occupational groups who have come to committees of this house or to parliament within the past few months to request that councils of one kind or another be set up to deal with their particular industry. I have them enumerated here.
We have had the tobacco growers come to a committee of this house and ask for some form of council in their industry to protect the growers. We have had the furniture trade come and ask for some code, if you wish to call it that, in their industry. Those engaged in the clothing trade have also come and asked for a code. The retail merchants of this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific are all wanting some form of code to give them an opportunity of merchandising their commodities on what they consider a fair basis. Then those on the farm raising hogs and cattle want some form of council in their industry to give them the protection which they have not got at the present time. Those who are engaged in the packing industry have also come to a committee of this house and requested some form of regulation to give them protection in their industry. Only within the past twenty-four hours we have had those engaged in the fruit industry come before a committee of this house asking that something be done to protect the industry by which they attempt to make a living.
Then, in milk production, already in the province of Alberta legislation has been passed for the fixing of prices, and similarly in Manitoba, and I believe that in the province of Quebec-if I am wrong I hope I shall be corrected-legislation has been passed to deal with the milk situation in that province. I could go on and say that this house on many occasions in the past has gone on record for some form of compulsion in regard to one industry or another. In 1929 when my hon. friends opposite were sitting on this side of the house they were opposed to compulsory unemployment and sickness insurance, *while the Liberal party was in favour of some form of compulsory unemployment and health insurance.
We can have no legislation of any kind for the well-being of the majority of the people without some form of compulsion. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I shall not deal with that aspect of the question.

I just want to say a word on the point raised by the leader of the opposition. If the producers get a higher price that will be reflected back in increased purchasing power for the labouring man. The leader of the opposition-I give him credit for sincerity-seems to be very fearful for the minority. I am a farmer. ceive for their products. I do not see anything dreadful about the position of the minority at all. When I do that, to a certain extent I destroy my own price as a competitor. I depress prices and, therefore, I destroy myself. I do not see anything very wrong with this bill. If a small minority does not come into the scheme, it will receive the same price as that received by the majority. There are bound to be certain individuals who cannot see their way clear to come in but if a majority thinks there is a possibility of raising commodity prices, those prices will be raised to the minority which has refused to come in. As far as the rights of minorities are concerned, may I say that the protection of the rights of minorities is a fundamental obligation upon parliament itself, as well as on all members of parliament. It is the particular obligation of a party that happens itself to be a minority. Sooner or later everyone comes to be in the minority with regard to something, and unless the rights of minorities are protected, liberty itself will soon disappear. I agree with my hon. friend when he says that the man in the community who seeks to lower standards and who is prepared to undersell by unscrupulous and unfair methods should be summarily dealt with, but I believe parliament itself has plenty of scope and power to pass the regulations necessary to deal with that class of persons and that kind of behaviour. I think it should be parliament and not local groups that should make the regulations that are to govern industrial and commercial practices. On the title of the bill there was a good deal of discussion that might more properly have taken place under this clause, and it seems strange that those who spoke about certain natural products included in this list are not here now to reaffirm their objections to certain items which it contains. The thing of outstanding interest to farmers on the prairies is grain, particularly wheat. Can the minister say whether under the conditions that now prevail in the marketing of wheat there is any possibility of this scheme being put into effect in the immediate future in connection with wheat? We know that the government has entered into certain commitments with other countries with respect to the marketing of wheat, and that is one thing that might be taken into consideration. Some-

Marketing Act
thing else that should be considered is that the marketing of wheat, as at present provided for, has developed over a long period of years. Since the beginning of the century certain grievances have arisen in connection with wheat marketing, and after a great deal of agitation on the part of the farmers with respect to some of these grievances the grain act was introduced regulating the conditions governing the marketing of wheat. That was followed by the Canada Grain Act. We would like to know whether there is any scheme that is to be put into effect that will in any way affect the operation of this very efficient body that has been created, the board of grain commissioners, a board that I think all the farmers of the west have perfect confidence in as regards its personnel. I believe the different boards of grain commissioners that have operated during the past have rendered very effective and efficient service. There was a great deal of unfair criticism against the former board. I was not by any means in sympathy with the criticisms that were directed against that board; I think they were mostly unfair and in some cases promoted by those who wished to cover up some of the mistakes that had been made by some of the organizations in carrying out the operation of selling wheat. But I think it is very important to know how this new board, if it is to be constituted, is to operate in connection with the present board of grain commissioners.
I want to state that the chief concern today is not in regard to marketing machinery in connection with our grain; it is in regard to getting markets for our grain and in this bill there is not the slightest indication of anything that will improve our markets. I know the claim has been made by those who advocate a one hundred per cent pool, that if they had only had control we would not have got into the difficulty in regard to marketing our wheat. As I stated before, any such claim as that is absolutely without foundation and absurd. I want to say this for the pools-and I have said it before- that they came upon a period of very hard times. Had the grain fluctuations been simply the normal, possibly the pools would have survived; they could not stand up under the tremendous fall in prices that took place. At the same time that does not justify those who are not only sympathetic but fanatically sympathetic toward the pools, in making the claim that they could have saved the situation if they had had one hundred per cent control. A more absurd claim could not be advanced.
I want to know from the minister just what the proposition is in regard to grain. Is there any likelihood under conditions as they prevail at present of advantage being taken, if it is deemed to be an advantage, of this bill to organize under it, or in view of the present situation is it wise, by including grain in this list, even to give the suggestion that the grain trade might be organized under the bill? As I have said already, to my mind the most important matter is not what our marketing machinery will be but where we are going to get markets for our grain and in this bill there is not the slightest indication of anything that will open markets to us. That is, after ail, the point in which the farmers of the west are most interested and it is one on which they are under a good deal of misapprehension. There is undoubtedly a certain amount of support from the west for a marketing bill, but it is on the supposition that the bill is one that will get .markets for our stuff. That is the thought which is uppermost in the minds of the farmers. That is true particularly in regard to grain; they suppose it is a bill that will do something towards securing markets for them, but in the bill there is not the slightest indication of anything of the kind. Therefore I would make the suggestion that in view of the present situation, grain be excluded from this bill. The government have made commitments. At the moment I am not going to say whether those negotiations that have been entered into and that have resulted in certain agreements may be good or bad; that is not the point at present. Those commitments have been made and in view of the present grain situation I suggest that it might not be wise even to indicate the possibility of the formation of a board to handle grain.

Just before the dinner hour, Mr. Chairman, we were dealing with section 2, subsection (e), which reads:
"Natural product" includes animals, meats, eggs, wool, dairy products, grainsand so on. I need not read the entire section. This is the amended subsection, by the way. The principle of this bill has been very throughly discussed on the second reading, and in fact I think the principle was discussed again on the short title. Heretofore I have not taken any part in the debate on this bill, and I do not believe I would have done so at this time except for the fact that the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) raised the question of wheat prior to the dinner hour. The hon. gentleman rose in his place and advocated that wheat should be left outside the scope of this bill. I was rather surprised to hear him express himself in that way, but he was just expressing the views that I find recorded in a publication issued in Winnipeg called The Country Guide, under date of May, 1934. This publication contains quite an extended article, which I do not propose to read, which I believe was prepared by the board of the United Grain Gorwers, who ask that wheat should be handled separately They go on to point out why grain should be excluded from the marketing act, and when I turn to the editorial page of this same issue I find the editor expressing himself in these words:
The opinion expressed elsewhere in this issue 'by R. S. Law, President of United Grain Growers,_ that grain should be excluded from the provisions of the natural products marketing bill, will commend' itself to the grain growers generally.
The hon. member for Lisgar expressed those sentiments fairly well; in fact I believe some of the arguments he advanced are quoted in this article almost as he gave them. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that I come from an agricultural constituency; the occupation of
[Mr. R. Weir.)
my people is farming, and they grow wheat almost entirely. So when you advocate leaving wheat outside the scope of this marketing act certainly it touches the people whom I represent. During the past week or so I have received a number of telegrams, which I have before me, from wheat pool committees, wheat pool directors and one from the mayor of a town, I have a letter as well. All these communications are along the same line, and I am going to read the letter in order to set forth the opinion of the grain growers in my section of Saskatchewan. The letter is addressed to myself under date of May 7, and reads:
Dear Sir:	[DOT]
It has just been brought to my attention that there is a strong movement to have wheat excluded from the operations of the natural products marketing act.
The farmers in this community look with strong disfavour on any attempt that may be made to have wheat excluded from the operation of this act.
I sincerely trust we can look to you to use your good offices and influence to have wheat included-
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) William Shaw.
That is a good sample of the telegrams and communications I have received. So far as my personal opinion goes I certainly think wheat should be included with the other natural products. The hon. member for Lisgar seemed to think there might be a possibility that the board of grain commissioners would be set aside. I do not. think that is likely to happen,, or that the Canada Grain Act will be set aside. I believe both the grain board and the grain act will be used under the new marketing bill. For several years we have had in western Canada a wheat pool which functioned very satisfactorily until the great slump in 1929. Since that time they have not been functioning as satisfactorily or as fully. I want to state here most emphatically-and I think I am stating the opinion of a great many farmers-that the private interests handling the grain are not indispensable. A great many farmers hold the view', which I share, that private interests controlling and handling our wheat, such as the United Grain Growers, are not by any means indispensable. In other words it is quite possible for the farmers of western Canada to handle their wheat independently of any such organization as the United Grain Growers or any other private body.
In order to acquaint the committee with what transpired last year in connection with the prices of grain in western Canada I am going to quote a few statistics which I have

Marketing Act-Mr. Carmichael
before me. I have here the prices for No. 1 Northern wheat in Winnipeg, the closing cash prices from January 1, 1933, to December 31 of the same year. Some interesting information is contained in those figures, and I think it bears very definitely on the question raised by the hon. member for Lisgar. I am not going to read the prices for the whole year, but I am going to deal with that portion of the season when the farmers of the west had very little grain in their possession and were marketing a comparatively small quantity of the 1932 crop. I will start with May 2, 1933. On that date the closing cash price for No. 1 Northern wheat at Winnipeg was 611 cents. On June 7 the closing price was 611 cents, so that over a period of thirty-six days the price remained fairly uniform. There were some fluctuations during that period, but the highest price was 651 cents while the lowest price was 611 cents; that was the entire spread during that period. On June 8, however, the price began to advance steadily; on that date it was 621 cents. Then jumping over to June 24 we find that it increased to 691 cents. That is an advance of 7f cents in sixteen days. Well, there is nothing very alarming about that. But on June 26,-I believe the 24th was a Saturday, and there was no market on Sunday the 215th,-on Monday the 26th, the price was 741 cents or an increase of 4f cents in one day.

I am bringing these points to the attention of the committee to emphasize the need for including wheat within the scope of this marketing bill. While the wheat pool is not functioning at the present time there are many farmers in western Canada who do not look upon it as a completely dead issue. It is true that in 1929 the wheat pool suffered financial reverses, but so did the private grain trade. There are men in western Canada who were involved in the handling of grain, either as private companies or private individuals, who suffered very heavy losses during the 1929 slump. The farmers in my constituency -and I believe I speak for the great percentage of the farmers in Saskatchewan-are expecting that times are going to become normal in the future, and perhaps in the not too distant future. When times become normal those farmers want the machinery at their disposal so that they may be able again to set up a farmers' marketing organization, if they choose to do so. There is no threat that they are going to do so, but they just wish to have the machinery available so that if they come to the point where they wish to organize a wheat pool and have it functioning as it has functioned in the past, they may have the machinery available for so doing.
I have made these remarks largely in answer to the expressions of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). I wondered why he took the stand he did take. I do not think he is so close to Winnipeg that he needs to reflect the viewpoint of the grain trade. I believe his is an agricultural constituency, although possibly it is not devoted to grain growing quite as extensively as is my own constituency. In any case, I do not pretend to give his reasons for advancing his arguments. I wish to emphasize my own argument, namely, that the people I represent want grains included in the marketing bill, and they insist upon wheat being included within the category of grains.

I was particularly interested this afternoon when the hon. minister stated that he was still open to suggestions and that the door would not be closed to further amendments. I have an amendment to offer to the section under discussion, but before presenting it I would like to make a few brief remarks.
Practically all, if not all, the speeches made on this bill since its introduction into the house have been made with regard to agriculture with the exception of the speeches that were made by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I am not at all surprised that that should be the case because, first of all, we have this bill in charge of the Minister of Agriculture, and secondly I believe practically all the demand for marketing legislation has come from agriculturists throughout the country.
Some member suggested this afternoon that this act will be an experiment in legislation. The suggestion I am going to make to the minister is that we start by dealing with one product at a time. I have recollections of the great difficulties we encountered in British Columbia before our Milk Producers Act and Natural Products Act in the province became law, and I think the government would be well advised to go a little slowly and deal only with agricultural products in the first place because if the difficulties met with are the same that we met with in British Columbia before we reached a definite conclusion, there will certainly be lots of complications in the administration of this bill throughout the length and breadth of Canada.
I am of the strong opinion that no demand has come from the fishing industry or the lumbering industry to come under this bill. Perhaps these products are being included in the bill with the idea of applying quotas to them. I do not expect that the hon. Minister of Agriculture would know a great deal of the difficulties or complications that might arise if the canning industry in British Columbia through its representatives were to ask

Marketing Act-Mr. Reid
for a board to be set up in that province. In British Columbia there are some forty-four canneries and well over five thousand gill net fishermen, most of whom own their gear and boats. The minister might say that these fishermen might get together and ask for a board to be set up, but so long as the bill provides that producers and marketers can come to the minister for a board my belief is that the marketers, the canned salmon industry, will probably be the first to ask for a board to be set up to control the product of fishing, namely, canned salmon. If such should be the case, I fear very greatly what might happen to the fishermen. The fishermen might want and did want to start a cooperative association of their own so that they could market their product. That association has not been in operation during the past year or so and were a board to be set up by the canners any movement on behalf of the fishermen for a cooperative association might very well be blocked, and the board that was acting on behalf of the canners might also control both the method of catching fish and the price of the product. I very much fear that that would not be in the interests of the fishermen.
I would ask	the minister to	tell me if	anyrequests	have	been made	on	behalf of	thefishing and lumbering industries to come under a bill of this kind. I know that the minister has had	lots	of requests	on	behalf of	thefarmers.	I know that the	apple growers,	the

The article to which I referred reads:

Marketing Act-Mr. Stevens
The Kyuquot Trotters' Cooperative x4ssocia-tion, which was recently admitted to the Cooperative Union of Canada, was organized in February, 1931, after a long period interrupted by strikes and price disputes with private buyers. According to a report published in the Canadian Co-operator, March, 1934, the membership in the new association has increased to 200 fully paid shareholders at $25 a share, and well equipped stations have been established at Kyuquot, Quatsino, Nootka, Ucluelet and Bamfield, covering the fishing grounds of the west coast of Vancouver island from cape Beale to cape Scott. President E. Larum reports as follows:-"We started chiefly as producers, but shortly after incorporation opened a general store on our Kyuquot and Nootka floats. We are this winter building a modern store and office at Kyuquot. Each of our members owns and operates his own boat and gear, with a value of from $1,500 to $3,000. The fishermen deliver their daily catches to the stations of the association, where they are weighed, iced, and held until transferred to the association's chartered diesel fish-packers running on schedule to the markets at Victoria, Vancouver and Seattle, U.S. The fishermen receive at each delivery a statement of the weights, and on return of the packers each received his payment according to market prices. In the three years the association has operated we have averaged a yearly production of 1,000.000 pounds of spring and cohoe salmon at an average yearly value of $150,000, with operating expenses $40,000 a year, much of which is duty on fish marketed in the United States and selling commission. The cooperative marketing of our fish proved a success right from the start, as well for the producers as the buyers. The fishermen have learnt to take better care of their fish, and have wholeheartedly given the management their support in putting a quality product on the market. There is nothing in the bill that will, as my hon. friend says, force this upon any group of operatives, either in the lumber or in the fishing industry. The bill is very clear in that regard; there must be a request for it from the operatives. The hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Neill) says, "But those interested in marketing may ask for a board."

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Well, that is quite true. I gather from the portion of the discussions I have heard that it is perhaps dangerous for me to suggest possible cases, because they will be seized upon and distorted into my declaring that it is the intention to do this or that. But if hon. gentlemen will permit me to illustrate, without charging me with having in the back of my mind, or suggesting that the Minister of Agriculture or any other member of the government has in the back of his mind, any intention of doing this or that, I could illustrate possible circumstances where it might be highly desirable and in the interests of industry to have some body or organization that could deal with a given situation. In what I am about to say, I wish it clearly understood

I emphasize this-that I am merely giving an illustration.
On the Pacific coast we have had very serious difficulty in connection with the export of herring, owing entirely to conditions beyond our control. I do not like to discuss this matter, and I hope it will be taken in the proper way. In the orient there has been a conflict of view between Japan and China- we will be frank about it. As a matter of fact China, which is a very important market for this product, imposed a local boycott upon herring coming from British Columbia because it was alleged that, in part or in whole, they were packed or handled, or owned or marketed by Japanese nationals. Now, that quarrel has nothing to do with us, but I can assure hon. gentlemen that it created a situation which

presented a very great difficulty to my own department. We had to handle it with a rather delicate touch, and I may say that it was perplexing. I can quite understand that under such circumstances the functioning of a board such as might exist under the act could very well handle a situation of that kind. In fact, I can see clearly where it might be of great advantage, without in the slightest degree interfering with the producer of herring. I will give another illustration.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Can the minister explain how the board could handle it to advantage?

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Yes. I will go a little
further, but again I warn my hon. friend that I am not stating what is likely to occur; I am merely speculating, trying to illustrate the situation. In the incident to which I have referred it was necessary for us to give assurances to certain sections of the market in the orient that the goods were not packed by a certain class of people in this country. As I say, in a measure it was none of our business; but, in the interests of the industry at the coast, we felt that it was our business as far as possible to secure the data and give the assurance, and with the assistance of the different parties in the transaction we were able to do so. In that way, I think, a board such as could be erected under this act would be of exceedingly great value, because its certificate would be accepted in all probability by the country to which the goods were destined.
I will give another illustration, and I ask the house not to request me for the moment to specify. I can do so if it is considered desirable, but I do not regard it as desirable to be specific in public. I have in mind a country in Europe-there are several, but there is one in particular which I have in mind, and an important one-which has placed a specific quota on imports into its market. Now, that is not something of our doing, but something which in their wisdom they have put into execution. Now when we approach the marketing season, obviously it is desirable as far as possible to arrange with the Canadian exporter to fit into the demands of that important market. That is done to the best of our ability. It is fraught with great difficulty and many perplexities, and there is great danger that if it is perpetuated and goes on year after year, or if the quota were narrowed a bit, it might be so perplexing as to involve perhaps unfairness to some exporters as against others.

Marketing Act-Mr. Stevens

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
You are referring to canned
salmon.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Yes, and I would ask that I be not requested to be too specific because it is not desirable. But there again it is necessary that we should have some organization to meet the exigencies with which we are confronted because of the actions of another country. I have in mind another situation, and it is applicable to fish, where there has been a contraction of the market, but where with the assistance of a board of this kind it might be possible to encourage or to develop export. I am myself giving that some study at the moment.
I can assure the committee that I can see changed conditions with which we are confronted all over the world in the matter of trade and the admission of goods into other countries, and with these changed conditions it may become absolutely imperative that we should have other machinery than the somewhat loose methods which under normal conditions might prove satisfactory or which in the past have proven fairly so.
Both hon. gentlemen who have preceded have referred to the products of the forest. I really see very little likelihood of there being any demand in that respect. Within the last year we have been confronted with a problem in connection with one of our largest manufacturing products-I do not wish to specify. We have been confronted with a condition of absolute chaos within the industry, and again this is due in large part to new conditions which have come into existence outside the control of the government of this country. We have had no machinery to deal with the situation. We have had no powers to meet it, but, I can easily appreciate that it is quite possible we might be of very great assistance to a Canadian group who were exporting in a large way from both coasts- and as a matter of fact there has been a condition of warfare between the two coasts in this particular product. Now, a marketing authority such as might come into being under this act, at their request, could act as mediator and conciliator between the two conflicting bodies of interest.
I express my own conviction-because I quite appreciate what both hon. gentlemen have in their minds-that there is no possibility, perhaps I should say no probability of there being any onerous obligations imposed upon any group against its will by reason of the passing of this act. I cannot conceive of anything of the kind being even remotely possible. Both hon. gentlemen who have
spoken rather emphasized the rights or liberties of the individual fisherman. I can say this, that with the principle that runs through this act I cannot see any possibility of anything being imposed upon any individual or class of operatives against their will. And as for there being any danger that the board might, in directing marketing, in its turn reflect or impose its will on the producer,- that is, I believe, the real apprehension in the mind of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni -one could conceive of an extreme condition under which it might go to the extent of doing that. But I should say that it would be completely foreign to the intent of the bill, and I cannot conceive of such an authority doing so. Certainly if that should happen there would easily be an opportunity to deal with it at the first session following such an act.
I feel impelled to say this-and I know I carry the judgment of my colleagues-that there is no thought in the mind of the minister who has charge of the bill or in the mind of any af his colleagues that there shall be erected a board which shall, in conflict with the wish of those whose business comes under it, act in any way antagonistic to their interest. I do see however where, in this changing condition with which we are daily confronted, such a board might be very useful in both these industries.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I appreciate the moderate tone which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has adopted and I will try to meet him in the same spirit. We agree with him entirely that the minister is animated by a proper desire in putting through this bill, and hopes and believes that nothing but good can come out of it. But when you are dealing with legislation you must contemplate, not what a minister designs and hopes and intends, but the use which other people may make of your legislation, human nature being essentially selfish.
As regards dried salted herrings for the oriental market, the minister said that the board might give certificates to the effect that the product was entirely handled by certain people, and so on. But that is done now. There is an inspection system under the Department of Fisheries and none of the product goes away without a certificate clearly indicating its quality and origin. The business is passing altogether into the hands of the orientals anyhow, and I am not particularly concerned to see that continue.
The minister was on sound ground when he brought in the question of the quota. That js above all one defence and justification and
Marketing Act-Mr. Neill

reason for the bill. If the British or some other nation say, "We will out off your quota of meat, butter, cheese, or whatever it may be", then we must have some machinery to handle that situation; and the argument of the Minister of Trade and Commerce was at least sound in that regard. But I would make this reply to him. Canned salmon is comparatively a small industry, in the hands of a few people, and it is held almost entirely on the Pacific coast. There are only two nations that have any suggestion of a quota at the present time. Last year I believe there were some thirty-four or thirty-five canneries operating in British Columbia. There is an association knows as the Canned Salmon Section of the British Columbia Manufacturers' Association, and I think there are only twenty-one or possibly twenty-two members. So that if it developed that a certain nation was putting a quota on canned salmon it would be easy for that private association to get together and regulate the supply and they would do it in a far simpler and easier way than it could be done through a board of this kind. That, I think, meets a good deal of the argument put forward by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I wish to give one further illustration to show why these people want to be left alone. Before I discuss that however I would refer to what the minister said in reference to lumber. He expressed the opinion that it was not at all likely that there would be any demand for a board. If he does not think that it will be asked for, and if the lumbering men have not asked for it, why not leave it out and have one trouble le.ss for the minister who will be in charge of the act? However, coming back to the cooperative association, and cooperation is supposed to be the basis of a good deal of this act, like all business men they must look ahead. In shipping fish to the market they engage diesel fish packers running on schedule. The contract, as I happen to know, for taking this fish in the months of May, June, July and August is made the previous fall, probably in November or early in December. Next fall, if this bill is in effect and this cooperative association undertakes to make a bargain to get these packers running to schedule, what guarantee will they be able to give? Suppose they want to ship a million and a half pounds of fish next year; they cannot guarantee that they will be allowed to ship the fish to the United States or anywhere else, nor can they guarantee any fixed price or quantity. What is the packer going to do? He will insist upon 
something definite. He will then be told that the consent of the board will be obtained. But it is hard to get the consent, of a board recently established to deal with conditions that will exist nine months in the future. Possibly they might have to go to the dominion board at Ottawa, and these men have neither time nor inclination, nor do they see the necessity for anything of the kind.
I cannot put the situation too strongly, and it is backed up by almost every representative of the fishermen in this house. Is not that full of significance to the minister? Would not some of them get up and say that in their particular districts the bill would be of benefit to the people they represent if that were really the case? The fishermen have made no request to the minister, so I wonder if he could not let this stand over and make some investigations of his own. Let him send out word to British Columbia through the acting Minister of Fisheries; let him ask the president of this cooperative association what he thinks. He is entitled to be heard.	I have not	his opinion	on	thesubject, but	this	would	affect him	or	atleast the association which he represents. Ask the canned salmon association; they would be entitled to give their views, but do not take such extremely drastic action in connection with an industry which is peculiarly ill adapted to come under the act and which does not appear to have been considered by the men	who	drew	it, without	giving
the matter serious consideration. It is quite evident that this act was framed having regard to agricultural products in the main, and it is not suited to the problem of fish.

Mr.	'Chairman,	in	my
constituency more people depend for a livelihood on fishing than on any other industry, and the fishing of sardine herring is the most important branch of that industry. The greater part of these herring go to the canning factories of Eastport, Maine, which pay only on the number of cases they can pack out of the fish they receive. Our fisher-ment have no chance at all to check up as to how many cases they do pack. Several times they have tried to form an organization in order to protect themselves, but with hundreds of weirmen it is easy for the factories in Eastport to persuade some of them to sell their fish on the basis of the number of cases packed, and as soon as one or two weirmen do it all the others have to follow. This marketing bill will give these fishermen the opportunity they have been looking for to unite, if they see fit to do so, in order to have some control not over prices but over

Marketing Act-Mr. Duff
the way their fish are marketed, and the quantity they have to market. To-day they may ship their fish to Eastport, and they may be told that the fish were not fit to pack or perhaps that they had to be put into fertilizer, for which they would get little return. Coming from a fishing constituency I think one of the first applications to this board will be from the sardine fishermen of Charlotte, and I would regret very much indeed to see the fishermen excluded from this act.

speechtext: In answer to the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Ganong) may I say that there is no need of any such act as this, if the fishermen of his constituency wish to get together and decide where they will sell their fish, to whom they will sell them or what quantity they will sell. That can be done by local organizations in a cooperative way, and this board is not necessary at all. So far as I am concerned I am going to take only a few minutes of the time of the committee, because I have come to two conclusions. The first is that a majority of the members of this parliament are going tc pass this bill, and the second is that the quicker the bill goes into operation.the better it will be, because inside of two or three months the government and members of parliament, as well as the fishermen, the lumbermen and the farmers w'ho come under this bill will be praying to God for the government to repeal the act.

That is what I say, but as I have not spoken in the committee previously perhaps my hon. friend will allow me to say a few words, because the province of Nova Scotia is interested in this legislation. I take it from what was said a moment ago by the Minister of Agriculture, who is in charge of this bill, and by his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce in reply to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) who moved this amendment striking out fish and lumber, that the fishermen need not come in under this bill unless they so desire. That is my first point. Now I turn to section 9 of the bill, which reads:
Notwithstanding that no petition in relation to any natural product has been filed, the minister may, if he is satisfied that the trade and commerce in the said product is injuriously affected by the lack of a local board to regulate such product, at any time propose a scheme for the marketing of such product

Surely if what was said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the Minister ol Agriculture a moment ago is correct, and no one need come under this scheme unless they
so desire, section 9 should be eliminated from the bill. My second point is that the minister said that no fishermen need come under this bill unless they so desired and unless a majority of the fishermen asked to do so. If that is so, and the fishermen, the farmers or the lumbermen need not come under the bill unless they wish, why is it necessary to put the producers to all the trouble set forth in this bill? For instance, the bill requires any or all persons engaged in the production or marketing of the regulated product to register their names, addresses and occupations, not only those who wish to come in under the scheme but everyone, whether they come under the scheme or not. They must register their names, addresses and occupations with the board. My hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) must laugh at that. How are you going to get the fishermen scattered from Ketchikan to the Fraser river to register? You will need an army of officials.

speechtext: A census.

You will have more than a
census; you will need the election enumerators they are going to appoint next month. Then every fisherman has to obtain a licence.

speechtext: Only those who of their own volition submit a scheme will be asked to do so. I think the hon. member is under the impression that these things are compulsory if there is no scheme. If the fishermen of Nova Scotia submitted a scheme which they thought would be to their advantage in the marketing of their fish, it is optional whether or not there will be a poll. There might be organizations set up in which there would be no poll and no compulsion, but we will take the case which I believe the hon. member has in mind. If the scheme submitted asked that a poll be taken in order that a vote might be secured to see if a majority were in favour of such a scheme, in which the others would be forced to participate, even then it might not be a part of that scheme to have these people registered or licensed. I agree with the. hon. member that in many cases it might be almost impossible to take a vote, but that would be dealt with at the outset. I wish to emphasize the fact that this registration would only come about when the scheme submitted by the producers themselves requested that this should be done. Perhaps it was not necessary for me to make these remarks, but I thought my hon. friend misunderstood me.

speechtext: I am afraid the minister does not understand the situation, so far as the fishing industry is concerned. Let me explain to him that there are at least two hundred localities or fishing ports in the province of Nova Scotia in each of which there are anywhere from, say, fifty to one hundred or more fishermen. In some cases perhaps there may be five hundred or one thousand fishermen. But, as I have said, there are two hundred different fishing localities. I understand from the minister that in each of these two hundred places the fishermen may get together and decide by their vote either to come in under the scheme, or to stay out. And if they do decide to come in under the scheme, then in those two hundred places there will be two hundred local boards and all situated in the province of Nova Scotia, and in the fishing industry alone. Is that right?
