That is what I am trying to
say to the minister, namely, that if the fishermen themselves, the government or the dominion marketing board decide there shall be only one local board-and for the sake of argument we will say it is to be at Halifax, which is fairly central-that board would be three or four hundred miles away from one part of the province, and about two hundred miles away from another part. I say to the minister that either he has got to have a local board in every fishing district-or practically every fishing district-or the thing would be absolutely unworkable, even if the scheme were good. That is the point.
And here is another point: Let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that in fifty fishing settlements scattered along the Nova Scotia coast line the fishermen met and a majority decided to come in under the scheme. Then, in the other one hundred and fifty settlements we -would suppose that the fishermen do not want to come in under the scheme; they do not meet, and they do not vote. Now
then, the minister is going to set up either fifty boards or one board for those fifty settlements, which have intervening settlements not operating under any scheme. How would it work if, as I said a moment ago, it is left to the fishermen themselves to decide, and if only fifty settlements out of two hundred decide to come in, the remaining one hundred and fifty deciding to stay out? Mr. Chairman, when the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) stated that it was the unanimous idea of the members of this house that lumber and fish products should be excluded from the operation of this act he certainly was not speaking for me. I am very much opposed to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). In my riding last year the conditions in the fishing industry were so bad that the provincial government of Manitoba held an investigation. It might surprise hon. members of this house to learn that there was perhaps over a million dollars' worth of fish produced in my riding a couple of years ago. If the amendment of the hon. member for New Westminster carries it will mean that the fishermen in my riding will have no redress whatever because most of their product is exported to the United States, and therefore it must come under dominion jurisdiction.
I think that the arguments of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni are not worthy of very much consideration, especially when he says that the hon. minister may permit an order to be made that no fish shall be exported from Canada. I never heard such an absurd statement in this house. You talk about human nature and its selfishness. Well, we have a situation existing in this country at the present time where citizens of Canada who are producing the products of the soil and working in the lumber camps or in the factories or in the fishing industry are practically in a state of starvation, in a state of slavery, and yet hon. members stand up in this house and talk about freedom. I heard the hon. member for Ontario the other afternoon lighting the lamps of all the failures of the past to try and prevent this government from enacting this progressive legislation. I think we have reached a situation in this country where the Liberal party as represented by the members in this house is no longer worthy of the name Liberal, and certainly they do not represent what I choose to call freedom. It seems to me that this marketing bill is somewhat anomalous in that it comes under the Minister of Agriculture. I presume that situation arises because the agriculturists have been the prime movers in requesting legislation of this- character, but it would seem as if the bill includes so many natural products that it might better come under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. original clause a natural product would not necessarily seem to have included, for example, such articles as wool, because wool is not in the narrow sense a natural agricultural product; it is one step removed from being a natural product. The same is true perhaps as regards honey, which is specified in the clause and certainly so with regard to lumber because while trees are natural products, I should think lumber is decidedly a secondary product. This second draft goes a great deal further than the original one, at least so far as a fair reading of the original draft would indicate. Now it includes the greater part of what is in the popular way styled as natural products.
Further than that, the amendment reads:
Any article of food or drink wholly or partly manufactured or derived from any such product.
The question arises why the derivatives should be limited to food and drink. With the exception of lumber they are so limited. Why we should say that there should be control over lumber made of trees and why we should not give any control over furniture made of lumber or, let us say, over clothes made of wool, I cannot quite see; it seems to me to be a very arbitrary limitation. Therefore I would beg leave to extend the scope of the act by moving:

Why should we not include the products of the mine? We have our coal mines, our gold mines, our copper mines, a great variety of mines and minerals. There seems to be no reason why we should bring in general legislation covering all those other departments of our natural products and deliberately leave out the one. It may very well be that no submissions have been made by the miners. We have been told that no submissions have been made by the fishermen or by the lumbermen. It may very well be the case that the clause will not be invoked in regard to the mines. Mr. Speaker, before moving the adjournment I desire to lay on the table two copies of the fifth report on Hudson bay insurance rates, 1934, by the imperial shipping committee.
The fifth report of the imperial shipping committee on Hudson bay marine insurance rates, which is made public to-day, indicates quite clearly that the underwriters are coming to recognize the comparative safety of this route, more particularly in view of the efforts the government is making to provide adequate aids to navigation and to maintain an efficient patrol service. The committee, on which Canada is represented by the High Commissioner for Canada, has been untiring in its efforts to obtain this recognition and have succeeded in no small measure. There is every reason to hope that as shipping over this route increases in volume and the demand for insurance grows, as it inevitably will, the more or less prohibitory rates that have been in effect heretofore will disappear.
The opinion of the committee, as expressed in this report, tends strongly to the view that during the season of open navigation the risk of casualty for vessels is little, if any, greater
Hospital Sweepstakes

on this route than on the St. Lawrence route, and they find it difficult to appreciate the reasons for the existing disparity between the rates for the suspension of warranty as between Churchill and Montreal. They, however, recognize that as long as the route is used by comparatively few vessels, as has been the case heretofore, the volume of insurance will be comparatively small and a single total loss would more than account for the profits of a whole' season. However, the committee are glad to be able to report that the joint hull committee, having in mind the experience so far obtained and the improvement of conditions effected by this government, have seen fit to recommend a reduction of ten shillings per cent on the insured value in the rates of additional premium to be charged for the suspension of warranty on this route. This reduction is in respect of vessels fitted with gyrocompass as well as vessels not so fitted. The existing advantage of ten per cent on vessels fitted with gyrocompass is maintained.
In view of the fact that the house is greatly interested in this matter, I felt this was the easiest way to bring it to its attention, rather than to make a statement outside of the house.
